title: The cut hair
hook: at the river Anoma he cuts his hair with his sword and puts on a simple robe

segments.voice: Yesterday, Channa and Kanthaka: the charioteer and the white horse who carried the prince out at midnight. Your line was someone rode with you. Who did you thank? Day thirty-nine.
screen: `CHANNA AND KANTHAKA — SOMEONE RODE WITH YOU.`

segments.voice: Have you ever cut your hair after something ended? A breakup, a new job, a hard year. The mirror shows someone lighter, someone starting over. Hair can carry who we've been. By dawn, the three riders reach a river. The later telling names it the Anoma. The prince gets down from Kanthaka on the sandy bank. He's still dressed as what he was: a prince, in silk and jewels, with long hair bound up in a royal topknot. He draws his sword. Channa watches. Today's word is what happens next.
screen: `HAIR IS WHO WE'VE BEEN.` → `DAWN AT THE RIVER.` → `HE DRAWS HIS SWORD.`

segments.voice: He takes his long hair in one hand and cuts through it with the sword. In the telling, what's left is short, curling to the right, and it stays that length for the rest of his life. Tradition links this to the small tight curls on statues of the Buddha. He throws the topknot into the air. Then he takes off his royal clothes and puts on a simple robe, the color of earth, like the wanderer from the fourth sight. He gives his jewels to Channa to take home. And in that moment, the prince is gone. There's a samana on the riverbank. The word for this is pabbajja. It means going forth: leaving the household life for the homeless one. It's still the word for it. In Theravada communities, when someone becomes a novice monk or nun, the ceremony is called pabbajja, and the head is shaved, as on that riverbank. In Myanmar, there's a ceremony for boys called shinbyu: they're first dressed up as princes, in silk and makeup, and paraded through town, and then their heads are shaved and they put on robes for a time, retelling this very morning with their own lives. What pabbajja teaches, even for people who never shave a head, is that some things we carry are costumes. The prince didn't hate his hair or his jewels. He just didn't need them for where he was going. There was simply less to carry.
screen: `CUT WITH A SWORD.` · `CURLS THAT NEVER GREW.` · `PABBAJJA — GOING FORTH.` · `BOYS DRESSED AS PRINCES, THEN ROBED.` · then, large: `LESS TO CARRY.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let your breath slow down. Now think of one small vanity you carry. Checking your reflection. A certain way you need to look before leaving the house. A number you check, likes or steps or followers. No need for shame about it. Picture setting it down on a riverbank, the way the prince set down his jewels. Just for today. Notice what changes, if anything, without it. Then rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Pabbajja. Going forth: leaving home life for the homeless one. Today, it's the name of the ceremony where a novice's head is shaved.
Your line: less to carry. Today, let one small vanity go, a mirror check, a scroll, a need to look a certain way, and notice who you are without it. Day thirty-nine.

howItsDone: In Theravada novice ordination, called pabbajja, the head is shaved and a robe put on; in Myanmar, boys going through shinbyu are dressed as princes before being robed as novices for a time.

fork.setup: you're on the riverbank at dawn, still in silk and jewels, a sword at your side. what do you do?
options: cut off your hair with the sword and put on a plain robe.
ride back to the palace before anyone wakes.

fork.reveal: he cuts his hair, throws the topknot into the air, and trades silk for an earth-colored robe. the prince is gone; a samana stands on the bank.

original.note: Pali: going forth, leaving home life; the novice ordination. Sanskrit pravrajyā.

trapdoor: what you thought: the prince got a haircut.
what it means: he set down the costume of his old life to go forth as a wanderer, with less to carry.
what a scholar hears: pabbajja (Sanskrit pravrajyā), from pa- (Sanskrit pra-, forth) + vraj, to go; novice ordination (pabbajja) is distinct from full ordination (upasampada).

sources.ref: Nidanakatha (introduction to the Jataka): the cutting of the hair at the river Anoma
Pabbajja Sutta (Sutta Nipata 3.1): the going forth

notes: Hair curling to the right and staying two finger-breadths long for life: Nidanakatha. Linking this to the curls in statues is a common traditional explanation; art historians give others. Confirm phrasing.
The topknot thrown into the air (caught by Sakka in the telling) is simplified; confirm.
Shinbyu in Myanmar: boys dressed as princes, paraded, then shaved and robed as novices for a time. Confirm.

Editor review (2026-10-01): softened 'which is why statues show curls' to 'tradition links'; 'across the Buddhist world' narrowed to Theravada communities (East Asian schools use translated terms); cut 'many boys' and 'everyone has one'; practice no longer tells the listener what they feel; hook trimmed of a sweeping claim.
